To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) multiple sclerosis is associated with a number of factors; 2) the factors have a postulated immune and environmental basis; and 3) there may be a pattern to the factors that characterizes patients and brings them into one or more causitive agents.

the risk of MS is higher in individuals with a history of smoking, a lower intake of vitamin D, a positive history of Epstein-Barr infection, or a history of recreational drug use, and lower in those with a history of oral contraceptive use, and that these associations appear to be independent of each other.

(1) MS patients have a higher risk-taking attitude than the general population; (2) MS patients have more risk-associated behaviour than the general population (including smoking, alcohol consumption, recreational drug use and sunburn); and (3) the higher risk-taking attitude is associated with the risk-associated behaviour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of factors that are associated with multiple sclerosis.
the identification and characterization of a pattern of risk-taking behaviour in MS patients that may be a unifying theme in the aetiology of the disease.
a unifying premise that multiple sclerosis (MS) is associated with risk-associated behaviour.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for a unifying hypothesis of causation for MS.
patients with MS are risk-takers, that this may be a unifying premise for MS, and that the most likely causative agents are viruses.
there is evidence of a link between risk-associated behaviour and MS, but no evidence of a link with risk attitude.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of MS increases as a result of a combination of genetic and environmental factors, which include smoking, alcohol, and viral infection.
multiple sclerosis is an infectious disease that has a strong genetic component.

the evidence is consistent with the view that patients with MS have a propensity to engage in risk-taking behaviour, and that this is associated with an increased risk of exposure to a causative agent or agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MS patient population appears to be a group of risk-takers.
the association between risk-taking and MS is strong.
the MS patient is not necessarily a risk-averse individual but rather a risk-taker who may be exposed to a causative agent.
